fact: SYNLawn's DIY installation guidelines call for 6-inch (60d) galvanized nails driven through the turf into the base; its materials page puts perimeter nails about every 6 to 8 inches, its installation steps nail every edge every 8 to 12 inches and stagger seam nails 8 to 12 inches apart, without crimping fibers under the nail heads.
quote: Nails: Nails should be placed about every 6-8” around the perimeter and staggered along seam. … Using 6” (60d) galvanized nails, nail one end of the turf section, tightly pulling other end in place. … All turf edges should be secured with nails every 8” to 12”, nailing through the turf and into the base. Be careful not to crimp the turf fibers under the nail heads. … Nail each side of the turf into the base, staggering the nails every 8”- 12” apart.
source_label: SYNLawn, DIY Installation Guidelines for SYNLawn Artificial Grass (PDF posted with the product listing)
notes: The manufacturer's own PDF, hosted on the retailer's product-document server. It gives two perimeter spacings (6-8 in on the materials page, 8-12 in in the installation steps); copy states both.

fact: SYNLawn's guide has the installer dig out 3 to 4 inches for the drainage base.
quote: Depending on your area, you will need to remove between 3”- 4” to create an adequate drainage base.
source_label: SYNLawn, DIY Installation Guidelines for SYNLawn Artificial Grass (PDF posted with the product listing)

fact: SYNLawn's guide says turf laid over concrete may be glued down, with no base required.
quote: Note: If turf is being installed over concrete, a glue-down method may be used and no base is required.
source_label: SYNLawn, DIY Installation Guidelines for SYNLawn Artificial Grass (PDF posted with the product listing)

fact: SYNLawn's guide has the sprinklers in the turf area removed and capped before work starts, and reminds installers to run drip lines to trees or plants that the old zone watered.
quote: make sure all the project site’s sprinklers are removed and capped off or cut the irrigation valves. Note: Don’t forget to run drip lines to trees or plants that were receiving water from this source.
source_label: SYNLawn, DIY Installation Guidelines for SYNLawn Artificial Grass (PDF posted with the product listing)

fact: ForeverLawn's landscape installation guidelines hold turf without boards using 6-inch 60D twisted-shaft galvanized landscape spikes about 8 to 10 inches apart and 3/8 to 1/2 inch in from the edge, with no blades trapped under a spike and no spike sunk so far that it dimples the turf; before seaming, spikes go down the middle of each roll parallel to the seam, and after seaming any area still unanchored is secured.
quote: 6” 60D twisted shaft galvanized landscape spikes if not using perimeter boards. … After the seaming is done, then any remaining unanchored areas should be secured. … When the seam looks good, take some spikes and anchor each roll so it doesn’t move. Do this by placing several spikes down the middle of the roll, parallel to the seam. … If using spikes: Space the spikes about 8”–10” apart. Place the top of the spike between the grass rows and about 3/8”–1/2” away from the edge of the grass roll. … Do not trap blades under the spike. Also, do not over pound or sink the spikes as this will create viable dimples in the grass.
source_label: ForeverLawn, General Landscape Installation Guidelines (M1374 Rev. 05/19)
notes: "viable dimples" is the source's wording (read: visible).

fact: With perimeter boards, ForeverLawn staples the turf to pressure-treated 2x4 boards set on edge, using galvanized narrow-crown staples 1 inch long with a 1/4-inch crown every 2 to 3 inches, within 1/2 inch of the board edge; free-standing boards are pinned with 1/2-inch rebar 18 to 24 inches long through holes about every 2 feet, and boards beside concrete are fastened into it with concrete screws or wedge anchors.
quote: Rebar–typically 1/2” that are 18”–24” in length if using rebar to secure board. … If using the pressure treated lumber (typically a 2”x4”) it will be installed on edge, not laying flat. … When the boards are installed adjacent to concrete (wall, house footer, sidewalk, driveway, etc.), use concrete screws or wedge anchor bolts to secure. … These holes are typically every 2’ on center. Rebar should then be pounded through the hole into the base beneath. … If using a perimeter board: Secure the grass to the perimeter boards using 1/4” narrow crown galvanized staples that are 1” in length. Staples are placed every 2–3” apart, and within 1/2” of the board edge using a pneumatic staple gun.
source_label: ForeverLawn, General Landscape Installation Guidelines (M1374 Rev. 05/19)

fact: ForeverLawn recommends perimeter boards on commercial installations and allows either boards or spikes around the perimeter of a residential one.
quote: It is recommended to use boards around the perimeter in commercial applications. You can use boards or just secure the perimeter of the grass with spikes in a residential installation.
source_label: ForeverLawn, General Landscape Installation Guidelines (M1374 Rev. 05/19)

fact: ForeverLawn's guidelines lay about 3 inches of crushed stone, 3/4 inch down to dust, and cap it with a 1-inch layer of fines.
quote: The size should be about 3/4” down to dust. This type of stone should be at a depth of about 3”. After this larger stone is brought in and compacted, a 1” layer of fines is used to cap the entire installation area creating a smooth finish.
source_label: ForeverLawn, General Landscape Installation Guidelines (M1374 Rev. 05/19)

fact: ShawGrass installation guidelines list landscape nails and spikes of about 3.5 to 10 inches, say local soils and the application decide the type and size, and space nails about every 6 inches along the perimeter and every seam; into a nailer board they use 1- to 2-inch galvanized nails or 1/4- to 1/2-inch staples, spaced closer.
quote: LANDSCAPE NAILS/SPIKES (approximately 3.5 – 10 inches in length) … There are a variety of spikes available ranging from plastic to galvanized/non-galvanized. Local soils will drive these considerations. Application will determine size of nail or spikes to use. Nails should be applied approximately every six inches along the perimeter of the installation, as well as along all seams to secure turf. Use nailer board nails one-to-two inches galvanized or staples ¼ inch – ½ inch. Shorter nail spacing may be required when using nailer boards.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: Shaw's guidelines list landscape spikes, timber spikes and sod staples for edges, spaced every 4 to 8 inches with the heads level with the turf backing, and describe a nailer board fastened to a concrete or asphalt curb that the turf is then nailed into.
quote: A. Landscape Nails and Spikes. Simply hammer landscape spikes, timber spikes, sod staples, etc. into the edge around the perimeter of the turf spaced every 4”-8”. (particularly if you are not planning on using an edging or curbing) The nail heads should be level with the turf backing to prevent turf from dimpling. … B. Nailer Board. When installed next to a concrete or asphalt curb, a nailer board / synthetic lumber can be installed (preferably in Step 2, Area Preparation) by nailing the board to the curb with concrete nails. The turf can then be nailed into the top of the installed nailer board with a landscape nail.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: Shaw's guidelines tell installers to secure the entire perimeter so pets can't pull the turf up or damage it.
quote: Secure the entire perimeter to prevent the synthetic turf from being pulled up or damaged by pets.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: Integriturf's installation guide calls nailing the most common method, every 4 to 6 inches around the perimeter and every 2 to 3 feet on center through the field with 5-inch 40D common or 6-inch electro-galvanized nails, and switches to a perimeter nailer board with 3/8-by-1-inch galvanized staples for playground areas or wherever nails are not advised.
quote: The most common method of securing the turf is to nail the turf every 4 to 6 inches around the perimeter and every 2 to 3 feet on center throughout the field using either 5-inch 40D Common, or, 6-inch electro-galvanized nails. For playground areas or applications where nails are not advised, install a perimeter nailer board (either pressure treated 2x4 or composite) around the perimeter and secure the turf edging pneumatically with 3/8-inch x 1-inch galvanized staples.
source_label: Integriturf, Synthetic Turf Installation Guide (PDF)
notes: Integriturf is a turf supplier; its guide is a general overview for homeowners and installers.

fact: Watersavers Turf's installation guide nails edges with 5- or 6-inch nails 3 to 4 inches apart and seams every 4 inches, makes nails through the middle optional at 12 to 24 inches, says turf expands and contracts with heat and cold so the perimeter must be tight, and warns that a nail driven too far leaves a noticeable dip.
quote: you will secure one end of the artificial turf with 5 inch or 6 inch nails and space them 3 – 4 inches apart along the edge. … Artificial turf expands and contracts in hot and cold weather so having a tight, secure perimeter is key. … We do not require that you place nails throughout the interior of the artificial grass. However, if you choose to do so, you can place them every 12 – 24 inches throughout the center. Never drive nails into base too far because this will create a noticeable dip. … Once seam is complete, nail along the seam every 4 inches to secure (do not counter sink).
source_label: Watersavers Turf, How to Install Artificial Grass
notes: A turf supplier's installation guide. The page also carries the supplier's phone line; never copy it.

fact: Watersavers Turf says its putting greens are installed differently, with no surface or perimeter nails.
quote: Putting Greens are installed differently. They have NO surface or perimeter nails.
source_label: Watersavers Turf, How to Install Artificial Grass

fact: PolyTurf's landscape installation manual says nails holding turf down should be checked routinely for working out from traffic, earth movement or other causes, and driven back in because protruding nails can hurt people and animals; it calls for galvanized nails because they do not rust.
quote: Whenever nails are used to hold down turf, they should be routinely checked to make sure they are not working out as a result of traffic, earth movement or other causes. Protruding nails can be a potential hazard to people and animals, so drive them back in if they stick their heads up! Always use galvanized nails as they do not rust.
source_label: PolyTurf, Installation and Maintenance Instructions: Synthetic Grass for Landscaping (2015)
notes: Manual dated by its copyright line (© PolyTurf 2015).

fact: PolyTurf screws turf edges to a perimeter edging board with 1-inch screws because screws come out more easily than nails when turf has to be pulled tighter to remove ripples, and uses optional 6-inch galvanized 60D nails in the field on slopes or every 4 feet, or about 12 to 15 inches apart where no sand infill is used.
quote: Screws: Small, 1” tarpon screws used to hold down the outer edges of the turf around the perimeter when turf is screwed into place on a perimeter edging board. Screws can be removed easier than nails if the turf needs to be pulled tighter due to rippling. Nails: (Optional) Used to pin down the turf on sloping areas. Optionally a 6” galvanized (60D) common nail is used throughout field of lawn, every 4’, if needed. … If no sand infill is used, insert 6” galvanized nails about 12” to 15” apart throughout the turf to hold it down.
source_label: PolyTurf, Installation and Maintenance Instructions: Synthetic Grass for Landscaping (2015)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse recommends 5- or 6-inch non-galvanized nails around the edges, saying they hold better as the installation ages because they expand over time.
quote: We recommend using 5 inch or 6 inch non-galvanized nails for securing your turf around the edges. As the installation ages, the nails will provide greater security as they will expand over time.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Installing Artificial Grass (FAQ)
notes: Directly contradicts PolyTurf's galvanized-only advice; the page presents both as makers' positions, not findings.

fact: K9Grass, ForeverLawn's pet turf line, says a proper pet-turf installation uses a plastic perimeter board anchored to the ground or an adjacent surface, with the turf secured by stainless steel staples every inch around all edges and penetrations.
quote: The proper installation for pet friendly turf will include a plastic perimeter board anchored to the ground or adjacent surface, then secured with stainless steel staples every inch around all edges and any penetrations.
source_label: K9Grass by ForeverLawn, Do pets chew dog friendly turf? (manufacturer FAQ)
notes: The sentence after the one in can-dogs-dig-through-artificial-turf.k9grass-edges. A manufacturer's installation standard for its own product; copy attributes it.

fact: A National Research Council Canada building digest explains that when soil freezes to a post or wall (adfreezing), the upward movement of growing ice lenses passes to it, soil then drops into the gap so it cannot settle back, and the problem can get worse from year to year.
quote: Movements in the soil resulting from ice lens growth can be transmitted to the structure if soil freezes to the foundation walls or supporting columns. The process is called adfreezing. … Frequently, also, soil material drops into the cavities produced by the heaving process so that the structure cannot settle back into its original position. Thus, the problem may get progressively worse from year to year, increasing the damage to both the foundation and the superstructure.
source_label: National Research Council Canada, Canadian Building Digest CBD-128, Adfreezing and Frost Heaving of Foundations (Penner and Burn, August 1970)
notes: Read in the NRC Publications Archive PDF (DOI 10.4224/40000858). The archive marks the series discontinued and historical. The digest is about foundations and posts; the page applies the mechanism to turf nails as its own reading and says so.

fact: The same digest's first remedy is to surround the post or wall with a drained zone of gravel or crushed stone that absorbs the uplift, which works only while the zone stays well drained; otherwise the stone freezes into a solid mass.
quote: The method best understood is based on the principle of separating the foundation wall or column from the surrounding soil with a drained zone of granular material such as gravel or crushed stone (Figure 2). In this way the uplift forces generated in the frost heaving soil are not transmitted to the foundation but lost in shear in the granular zone. This zone must be well drained or the granular material will freeze into a solid mass.
source_label: National Research Council Canada, Canadian Building Digest CBD-128, Adfreezing and Frost Heaving of Foundations (Penner and Burn, August 1970)
